newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Gas producers seen hindering free Australia market.
newsitem.headline: Gas producers seen hindering free Australia market.

text.p: A free market in electricity in Australia could lead to the eventual development of a potentially volatile free market in natural gas, an industry conference heard on Thursday.

But doubts were expressed over when this might occur -- despite a timetable laid down by the government of the east coast gas-producing state of Victoria -- because of tough bargaining by big energy producers.

Speakers told the Gas and Electricity Risk Management Conference the birth of a spot market in pipeline gas would be essential for the development of the free gas market which the Victorian government has stipulated should begin in September 1998.

While free competition between gas retailers is seen likely, conference speakers showed the industry is torn by debate about whether the free market push will survive tough terms said to be insisted on by Victoria's Bass Strait consortium.
Bass Strait gas is produced by a 50/50 Exxon Corp - Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd joint venture.

Similarities between gas and electricity as power sources ended with the two main points that gas could be stored -- electricity could not -- and that the gas industry included big private enterprise suppliers, conference speakers said.
"There will be no development in gas derivatives without a liquid spot market," Julian Turecek, energy trader for Boral Energy, a unit of Boral Ltd, told the conference.

Australia had many discovered but undeveloped gas fields, it had the precedent of wholesale electricity reform as well as storage and other facilities able to support an integrated gas market, he said.
But oligopoly of supply was a hindering factor, with only two major producing gas basins, Bass Strait and central Australia's Cooper Basin, owned by a consortium led by Santos Ltd, he said.
"Concentration of private players in the production sector of the industry will tend to slow the reform process relative to electricity reform," he said.
"They (large suppliers) have no interest in price transparency and like to say there is limited supply," he said.

"While I believe that Australia's gas industry has much latent potential, (this) will only be materially realised if and when a competitive market emerges," Glen Gill, general manager, energy supply and market development, Allgas Energy Ltd told the conference.

"The recent privatisation results surrounding Victoria's electricity industry illustrates the aggressive positioning of private companies when there is a high degree of confidence in the market structure of any given commodity," he said.
"The establishment of a spot gas market in Australia is one of the basic building blocks toward a gas market," he said.

But Gill went on to describe Australia's gas market so far as "as shallow as it gets", with essentially one marketing joint-venture representing one supply basin captive to one pipeline and selling to one gas utility representing a franchise or captive customers.
The volatility of gas contracts on New York's NYMEX, many times greater than for oil, suggested the potential for active gas derivative products in Australia, speakers said.
But with gas prices presently held steady through long-term contracts, when Australian gas derivatives might begin trading was not known, Turecek said.
